# The goal: post-selection inference for the standard trial analysis {#sec-target}

## Identified subgroups and the winner's curse {#sec-winners-curse}

Randomized trials are designed and powered to estimate an overall treatment
effect, yet some of their most consequential questions are subgroup questions:
is there an identifiable set of patients in whom the treatment is harmful, or in
whom an apparently inert treatment works? When such a subgroup is *identified
from the trial data* rather than prespecified, the act of identification
contaminates the estimate. A subgroup chosen because its estimated effect is
extreme has, by construction, an effect estimate biased toward extremity — the
winner's curse of subgroup search — and a confidence interval computed as if the
subgroup had been prespecified under-covers [@leon2024]. Post-selection
inference is the repair: a point estimate purged of the optimism that selection
injected, and an interval that carries the variability of the selection itself.

## The target of inference: the standard Cox and GLM analyses {#sec-standard-target}

A post-selection method is defined as much by *what* it makes inference about as
by how. We take the target to be, *for better or worse*, the **standard
analysis**: the treatment effect that would be reported had the subgroup been
prespecified. For a time-to-event outcome this is the partial-likelihood
coefficient — the log hazard ratio — of a within-subgroup Cox
proportional-hazards model [@cox1972]; for binary, count, and continuous
outcomes it is the within-subgroup GLM treatment coefficient: the log odds
ratio, the log incidence-rate ratio, the mean difference. Writing
$g \subseteq \{1,\dots,N\}$ for a candidate subgroup and $\beta(g)$ for the
population coefficient of the trial's working model restricted to $g$, the
reportable object is $\hat\beta(\widehat H)$ — the standard-analysis estimate
evaluated at the identified subgroup $\widehat H$ — and the inferential goal is
a de-biased estimate of $\beta(\widehat H)$ with an interval that is valid in
the presence of the selection that produced $\widehat H$.

This commitment is deliberate, and it is not a claim of causal optimality.
Hazard ratios are non-collapsible; odds ratios share the property; a working
model is a working model. The case for the standard analysis is institutional
and pragmatic: it is the inferential currency of randomized trials — the scale
on which they are designed, monitored, reported in primary publications, and
read by regulators and clinicians. A flagged subgroup must ultimately support a
claim of the form *"had this subgroup been prespecified, its analysis would have
shown this effect, with this precision."* The claim is stated in the trial's
currency, so the inference must be delivered in it. "For better or worse" is
meant exactly: this paper provides valid post-selection inference for the
estimand trials actually report, not an argument that this estimand is the
ideal causal summary.

The second half of the commitment is *interpretable membership*. Take a
patient's baseline covariates to be $x = (x_1, x_2)$ (case example case carried through @sec-fs-family). The
subgroups considered here are defined by explicit thresholds on those
covariates: "$X_1 \le c_1$ and $X_2 > c_2$" -- a criterion a clinician can evaluate 
from the two measurements alone, without a fitted model in hand.
Contrast with a score-thresholded set $\{x : \hat\tau(x) > t\}$, where $\hat\tau$ is
an estimated covariate-conditional treatment-effect surface and $t$ a cutoff. As
an estimation device this may be excellent, but its *membership rule is the
model*: to decide whether the same patient $(x_1, x_2)$ belongs, one evaluates
the fitted surface $\hat\tau(x_1, x_2)$ and compares it to $t$, and the boundary
is whatever level set $\hat\tau$ traces in the $(x_1, x_2)$ plane — in general a
curved, data-dependent region with no closed-form description, not a rectangle
of interpretable cutoffs. That surface $\hat\tau(x)$ is exactly the
covariate-conditional effect the modern subgroup identifiers of @sec-ml-targets
estimate, which is why their natural output is a model-defined set rather than an
interpretable rule — and, as the next subsection develops, why the estimand they
target departs from the standard analysis. The reportable unit throughout is the
triple (interpretable definition, standard-analysis effect, valid post-selection
interval).

## What modern identifiers target instead {#sec-ml-targets}

The machine-learning literature on heterogeneous treatment effects supplies
powerful subgroup *identifiers*, but they are built around different estimands
than the one above — a point that matters because it determines what their
selection statistics are.

Generalized random forests and causal forests
[@wagerathey2018; @atheytibshiraniwager2019] estimate conditional average
treatment effects on the difference-in-means scale; their survival extension,
causal survival forests, targets differences in restricted mean survival time,
or in survival probability at a fixed horizon — not the Cox log hazard ratio.
The difference-in-natural-parameters (DINA) framework of @gao2025 targets the
*causal contrast of natural parameters*,
$\tau(x) = \eta_1(x) - \eta_0(x)$ — a per-patient log odds ratio, log rate
ratio, mean difference, or log hazard ratio contrast — estimated with
orthogonalized, cross-fitted machinery in the R-learner tradition
[@robinson1988; @niewager2021; @chernozhukov2018], and it proposes subgroups by
ranking the subgroup mean $\bar{\hat\tau}_g$ of the fitted per-patient effects.
The DINA scale coincides with the standard analysis's scale — a coincidence
this paper will exploit — but the estimand and the selection statistic do not:
a covariate-conditional causal contrast averaged over a subgroup is not the
within-subgroup fitted coefficient of the trial's working model, either as a
population quantity or, what matters most for selection, as a random object
under resampling. Virtual twins [@foster2011] and modified-covariate methods
[@tian2014] likewise rank model-derived individual scores.

None of this is a criticism. These are arguably better causal estimands and
certainly strong discovery engines. The difficulty is downstream. When a
subgroup is *selected* by ranking one statistic but *reported* through another
— the standard analysis — the selection event and the reported quantity live on
different probabilistic objects, and post-selection inference for the report
must either model the selection that was actually performed or align the
selection with the report. The resolution developed later in the paper (the
alignment section, spine §5) is the second: such procedures are treated as
*candidate generators*, and their selection is re-ranked on the inferential
effect. For the present section the point is the framing itself: the goal of
inference is the standard analysis, and the identification machinery — whatever
it is — is in service of that goal.

## This paper {#sec-this-paper}

Our starting point is the post-selection correction of @leon2024 for forest
search under the Cox model: a bootstrap de-biased estimate that subtracts the
average of *two* resampling discrepancies — the discrepancy at the
*re-selected* subgroup of each resample, which is the selection optimism in the
lineage of @harrell1996, and the discrepancy at the *observed* selected
subgroup, the estimator's own finite-sample bias there, a term the Harrell
correction omits — together with an infinitesimal-jackknife variance
[@efron2014; @wagerhastie2014] that treats the corrected estimate as a bagged
estimator. This paper generalizes that construction along three axes: from
forest search to any identification procedure whose selection is, or is
re-ranked to be, a functional of the per-candidate standard-analysis effects;
from the Cox model to the GLM family on the natural-parameter scale; and from a
literal bootstrap re-run of the search to a fast, refit-free
multiplier-resampling computation that reproduces the bootstrap correction —
point estimate and interval — to first order, conditional on the candidate
family. Section @sec-fs-family develops the structural property that makes all
three possible, in the simplest instance that exhibits it.

# Forest search as a fixed candidate family {#sec-fs-family}

Forest search [@leon2024] is an exhaustive identification procedure: enumerate
an interpretable family of candidate subgroups, evaluate each with the trial's
own analysis, screen on effect size and internal replicability, and select
among the survivors. We present it here in its simplest non-trivial instance —
two continuous baseline covariates — because this instance isolates, without
clutter, the structural property the rest of the paper rides on: the candidate
family is **fixed**, and consequently a bootstrap of the *entire search*
collapses, to first order, into a re-ranking of jointly perturbed
standard-analysis coefficients.

## The candidate family from two covariates {#sec-family-construction}

Let $X_1$ and $X_2$ be two continuous baseline covariates.^[We say *baseline
covariates*; the package interface, following @leon2024, calls the candidate
subgroup-defining variables *confounders* (`confounders.name`).] For each,
place a grid of candidate cut points,
$c_{1,1} < \cdots < c_{1,k_1}$ for $X_1$ and
$c_{2,1} < \cdots < c_{2,k_2}$ for $X_2$, at prespecified locations of the
observed distribution — the package's default cut set for a continuous
covariate is the mean, median, and quartiles ($k_j = 4$), and a $J$-quantile
grid placing $k_j$ cuts at the $m/(k_j+1)$ empirical quantiles,
$m = 1,\dots,k_j$, is the general alternative. Each cut point defines the two
one-sided conditions it can generate, so the base set of subgroup-defining
conditions is
$$
\mathcal B \;=\; \big\{\, \mathbf 1\{X_j \le c\},\; \mathbf 1\{X_j > c\}
\;:\; c \in \mathcal C_j,\; j = 1,2 \,\big\},
\qquad |\mathcal B| \;=\; L \;=\; 2\,(k_1 + k_2),
$$ {#eq-base}
and the **candidate family** is every conjunction of at most two distinct
conditions,
$$
\mathcal F \;=\;
\big\{\, B \;:\; B \in \mathcal B \,\big\}
\;\cup\;
\big\{\, B \wedge B' \;:\; B, B' \in \mathcal B,\; B \neq B' \,\big\},
\qquad
|\mathcal F| \;\le\; L + \binom{L}{2}.
$$ {#eq-family}
Its members read as clinical criteria: one-sided sets $\{X_1 \le c\}$; corners
$\{X_1 \le c,\, X_2 > c'\}$; and, from two cuts on the same covariate, intervals
$\{c < X_1 \le c'\}$. The bound in @eq-family is not attained — empty
intersections (the two sides of one cut) and candidates failing minimum
subgroup-size and minimum-event guards are dropped — and with the default four
cuts per covariate, $L = 16$ and $|\mathcal F| \le 136$. The construction
generalizes verbatim to conjunctions of up to $\texttt{maxk}$ conditions,
$|\mathcal F| \le \sum_{k \le \texttt{maxk}} \binom{L}{k}$; two suffice for
this section.

The property to register is what $\mathcal F$ does *not* depend on. The family
is determined by the covariate cut grids alone — before any outcome model is
fit, before treatment assignment is consulted. It does not depend on outcomes,
on fitted effects, or on any learned surface. Throughout the paper, *fixed
family* means precisely this: the list of subgroup definitions @eq-family is
one fixed object, and any resampling of the data re-evaluates the *same* list
rather than generating a new one. (Cut locations computed from observed
covariate quantiles are held fixed under all resampling in this paper; the
family is the list of definitions so formed.)

## The per-candidate standard analysis {#sec-percand}

Each candidate receives the trial's own analysis. For $g \in \mathcal F$, fit
the working model to the members of $g$: under proportional hazards,
$\lambda_i(t) = \lambda_{0,g}(t)\,\exp\{\beta(g)\,A_i\}$ for $i \in g$, with
$A_i \in \{0,1\}$ the randomized treatment; for a GLM outcome,
$g_{\mathrm{link}}\big(\mathbb E[Y_i \mid A_i]\big) = \alpha_g + \beta(g)\,A_i$
— optionally covariate-adjusted in either case. The estimate $\hat\beta(g)$
solves the within-subgroup score equation
$\sum_{i \in g} \psi_i(\beta; g) = 0$, and the per-subject empirical influence
is the dfbeta
$$
\mathrm{db}_{g,i} \;=\; \mathcal I_g^{-1}\,\psi_i\big(\hat\beta(g);\, g\big)
\;\approx\; \hat\beta(g) - \hat\beta_{(-i)}(g),
\qquad
\sum_{i \in g} \mathrm{db}_{g,i} = 0,
$$ {#eq-dfbeta}
with $\mathcal I_g$ the within-subgroup observed information. The sum of
squared influences,
$\sigma_{D,g}^2 = \sum_{i \in g} \mathrm{db}_{g,i}^2$, is the robust
(sandwich / infinitesimal-jackknife) variance of $\hat\beta(g)$
[@linwei1989; @white1980; @efron1982]. Orientation is fixed once: harm
corresponds to $\beta > c$ on the model's own scale, with $c$ the log of a
ratio threshold for ratio measures and the threshold itself for a mean
difference.

## The splitting-consistency screen {#sec-consistency}

A candidate is admitted not on the size of its estimate alone but on the
*internal replicability* of that estimate. The criterion of @leon2024 is a
repeated random split: divide $g$ into two halves by independent fair coins,
refit the working model on each half, and call the split **consistent** if both
half-estimates exceed the consistency threshold $c_{\mathrm{cons}}$; over many
splits, the consistency rate $p_{\mathrm{cons}}(g)$ is the fraction of
consistent splits, and $g$ is admitted if
$p_{\mathrm{cons}}(g) \ge p^\star$ (default $0.90$) alongside the screening
requirement $\hat\beta(g) \ge c_{\mathrm{screen}}$ on the full fit (defaults
$c_{\mathrm{screen}} = \log 1.25$, $c_{\mathrm{cons}} = \log 1.0$).

As defined the criterion costs on the order of $10^3$ refits per candidate and
is statistically opaque; a first-order analysis removes both objections. Encode
a split by inclusion indicators $Z_i \in \{0,1\}$ and expand the half-sample
score about $\hat\beta(g)$ (each half carries half the information): the two
half-estimates form a mirror pair around the full fit,
$$
\hat\beta^{(A)}(g) - \hat\beta(g) \;\approx\; \sum_{i \in g} G_i\,\mathrm{db}_{g,i}
\;=:\; D_g,
\qquad
\hat\beta^{(B)}(g) - \hat\beta(g) \;\approx\; -\,D_g,
\qquad
G_i = 2Z_i - 1,
$$ {#eq-mirror}
so the fair-coin split *is* a Rademacher multiplier bootstrap of the subgroup
estimating function, and the split perturbation $D_g$ has conditional variance
exactly $\sigma_{D,g}^2$, the robust variance of $\hat\beta(g)$. From this one
object follow the consistency screen's two readings, both derived in
@sec-appendix-multiplier: a *closed form* for the consistency rate, computed
without any splitting, and a *calibration* that makes admission at level
$p^\star$ exactly the requirement that the one-sided $(1+p^\star)/2$ robust lower
confidence bound for $\hat\beta(g)$ clear the threshold — for the default
$p^\star = 0.90$, that the effect exceed $c_{\mathrm{cons}}$ by $1.645$ robust
standard errors. The criterion is then evaluated by literal splitting or,
equivalently, by the multiplier resampling it linearizes to (the package's
`resample` method); that appendix also places the fair-coin split alongside its
score- and bootstrap-resampling cousins, the simplest instance of the apparatus
the post-selection correction reuses.

What carries forward to the bridge of @sec-bridge is the structural reading:
**per candidate, the estimate and its consistency screen are functionals of one
fitted model — its coefficient $\hat\beta(g)$ and its influence values
$\{\mathrm{db}_{g,i}\}$.**

## Selection {#sec-selection}

Admission is per candidate; identification *selects*. Collecting the screen and
the calibrated consistency requirement into per-candidate thresholds
$t_g = \max\big(c_{\mathrm{screen}},\; c_{\mathrm{cons}} +
z_{(1+p^\star)/2}\,\sigma_{D,g}\big)$, the procedure applies a deterministic
rule to the candidate effects — among the admitted
$\{g : \hat\beta(g) \ge t_g\}$, take the largest effect, or the most consistent
candidate, with subgroup size breaking ties — which we write as a **selection
map** acting on the vector of candidate effects:
$$
\widehat H \;=\; \mathcal S\big(\{\hat\beta(g) : g \in \mathcal F\}\big).
$$ {#eq-selmap}
The particular rule matters less than its two structural properties: $\mathcal
S$ is deterministic given the candidate effects (with the $\sigma_{D,g}$
entering only through the fixed thresholds $t_g$), and it **ranks on the
inferential effect** — the same $\hat\beta(g)$ the report is about. The naive
report $\hat\beta(\widehat H)$ is then optimistically biased: $\widehat H$ was
chosen for the extremity of the very quantity being reported.

## The bridge: a fixed family turns re-selection into resampling arithmetic {#sec-bridge}

The de-biasing of @leon2024 is a bootstrap of the *search*: each resample
re-runs enumerate–screen–select, so the resampling distribution carries not
just re-estimation of a fixed subgroup but **re-selection** — on each resample
a possibly different winner. The question this subsection answers is how the
multiplier resampling already introduced — the same object underlying the
consistency screen and the textbook bootstrap of a single Cox or GLM
coefficient — captures that re-selection aspect. The answer is the fixed
family, in four steps.

**(i) One resample is one weight vector.** A nonparametric bootstrap resample
does not manufacture new subjects: it assigns subject $i$ a multiplicity
$K^{*}_{bi}$ (its count in resample $b$, $\sum_i K^{*}_{bi} = N$), and
refitting candidate $g$ on the resample means solving its score equation with
each member's contribution weighted by $K^{*}_{bi}$. Because the unweighted
scores sum to zero at $\hat\beta(g)$, only the *centered* weights
$G_i(b) = K^{*}_{bi} - 1$ perturb the solution, and to first order the refit is
a dot product with the influence values:
$$
\hat\beta^{*}_b(g) - \hat\beta(g)
\;=\; \sum_{i \in g} \big(K^{*}_{bi} - 1\big)\,\mathrm{db}_{g,i} + o_p\!\big(n_g^{-1/2}\big)
\;=:\; D_g(b).
$$ {#eq-boot}
This is the same object as the split perturbation in @eq-mirror under a
different weight law — centered multiplicities in place of Rademacher signs.
Both laws are mean-zero with unit variance, and with centered-Poisson weights
($K^{*}_{bi} \to \mathrm{Poisson}(1)$, the bootstrap's own multiplicity law)
@eq-boot is the infinitesimal-jackknife linearization of the nonparametric
bootstrap [@efron2014]. The consistency screen and the bootstrap of a Cox/GLM
coefficient are one resampling object under two multiplier laws.

**(ii) With the family fixed, re-running the search is re-applying the rule.**
Now bootstrap the search itself, and ask what a resample can change. The family
cannot change: $\mathcal F$ is the same fixed list of definitions
(@sec-family-construction), so the candidates evaluated on resample $b$ are the
candidates evaluated on the original data. The per-candidate analyses change
only through the weights — that is, through @eq-boot. The rule is the same
deterministic map $\mathcal S$. Therefore "re-run the entire search on resample
$b$" collapses, to first order, into "re-apply the rule to the perturbed
effects":
$$
\widehat H^{*}_b \;=\;
\mathcal S\big(\{\hat\beta(g) + D_g(b) \;:\; g \in \mathcal F\}\big),
$$ {#eq-reselect}
with the thresholds $t_g$ held at their observed values. This is the
re-selection aspect, captured: the bootstrap does not merely re-estimate the
chosen subgroup, it re-*chooses* — and @eq-reselect says that over a fixed
family, re-choosing is a deterministic functional of exactly the quantities the
single-subgroup bootstrap already controls. Selection introduces no new
approximation: the only expansion anywhere is @eq-boot, the same dfbeta
linearization that underwrites the consistency screen @eq-closed.

**(iii) One shared vector makes the competition honest.** Selection is a
competition: the winner of draw $b$ is decided by comparisons among candidates,
hence by *differences* $D_g(b) - D_{g'}(b)$, never by one candidate in
isolation. In a real resample there is one draw of the data, and every
candidate is re-fit against the same multiplicities; the arithmetic mirrors
this by broadcasting a **single** multiplier vector to all candidates on each
draw, which endows the perturbations with the candidates' true overlap
covariance,
$$
\operatorname{Cov}\big(D_g(b),\, D_{g'}(b) \,\big|\, \text{data}\big)
\;=\; \sum_i \mathrm{db}_{g,i}\,\mathrm{db}_{g',i}.
$$ {#eq-overlap}
Two nearly identical candidates are pushed by the same weights on their shared
members, which cancel in the difference, so the winner flips between them only
on draws that genuinely favour one — exactly the bootstrap's behaviour.
(Independent per-candidate perturbations would let near-duplicates trade places
far too often, manufacturing selection variability the bootstrap never
produces.) Computationally, everything is one matrix product: stacking the
influence columns into $\mathbf B_{\mathrm{eff}} \in \mathbb R^{N \times S}$
and the multiplier draws into $\boldsymbol\Xi \in \mathbb R^{N \times B}$, the
product $\mathbf P = \mathbf B_{\mathrm{eff}}^{\top}\boldsymbol\Xi$ holds every
candidate's perturbation on every draw — the data enter only through
$\mathbf B_{\mathrm{eff}}$, the randomness only through $\boldsymbol\Xi$.

**(iv) What this buys, and what to call it.** On each draw the re-selected
winner carries its own perturbation $D_{\widehat H^{*}_b}(b)$; because the rule
rewards large perturbed effects, the winner's perturbation is positive on
average, and that average *is* the selection optimism — subtracting it,
together with the same-draws term at the observed $\widehat H$, is exactly the
two-term León correction, developed with its infinitesimal-jackknife interval
in the correction section (spine §§3–4). The point of the present section is
structural, and it is the sense of *procedure-agnostic* in our title: nothing
in steps (i)–(iii) used how $\mathcal F$ was constructed or why $\mathcal S$
ranks as it does. The construction requires precisely two things — a **fixed**
family of subgroup definitions, each carrying its standard analysis
$\big(\hat\beta(g), \{\mathrm{db}_{g,i}\}\big)$, and a selection that is a
**functional of those candidate effects**, @eq-selmap. Forest search satisfies
both natively, which is why it is the clean first instance; any identifier that
can be expressed in this form inherits the identical post-selection machinery,
whatever generated its candidates. Identifiers that rank on a *different*
statistic (a fitted per-patient effect, a doubly-robust score) or whose family
is *regenerated* by each resample do not satisfy the conditions as stated;
bringing them under the template — by re-ranking their qualifying candidates on
the inferential effect, conditional on the proposed family — is the subject of
the alignment and scope sections (spine §§5–6).

Decision drafted: the DINA casting is *held off*, and this section runs
entirely on the standard-analysis coefficient and its dfbeta. Rationale:
(a) the bridge's punchline — selection as a functional of the per-candidate
standard analyses over a fixed family — *is* the procedure-agnostic template,
and stating it without DINA vocabulary keeps the template's two requirements
visible, which is what the alignment section then shows DINA/GRF violating
natively; (b) introducing $\tau(x)$ and $\bar{\hat\tau}_g$ here would put two
effect notions on the page before the reader needs them, and the worked
winner-flip example lands harder when the native statistic arrives as the new
object; (c) the unifying service DINA does perform — one natural-parameter
scale across Cox/logistic/Poisson/Gaussian, with $\beta(g)$ recognized as the
subgroup's constant DINA under the indicator basis — belongs to the
estimand-layer section (spine §2), where it is the point rather than a
digression. If the alternative is preferred, the natural insertion is a short
paragraph after @eq-dfbeta noting that $\beta(g)$ is the subgroup DINA of
@gao2025 (indicator basis), with the alignment caveat deferred; that variant
can be produced on request.
:::

# Appendix: The splitting-consistency screen as the simplest multiplier resampling {#sec-appendix-multiplier}

This appendix works out the splitting-consistency screen of @sec-consistency as
the simplest instance of the multiplier resampling the main text uses for
post-selection correction. The structure is the same in both: perturb the
candidate's fitted effect by a mean-zero, unit-variance multiplier vector and
read off a functional of the result. Only the question differs — here, whether a
single candidate replicates under a $50/50$ split; in @sec-bridge, which
candidate is re-selected under one shared perturbation and how much selection
inflates its effect. Reading the screen this way is the cleanest entry point to
the apparatus, which is why it is collected here rather than carried through the
main argument.

## From the fair-coin split to the closed form {#sec-am-closed}

Start from the linearized split of @eq-mirror: the two half-sample estimates are
a mirror pair $\hat\beta(g) \pm D_g$ about the full fit, with split perturbation
$D_g = \sum_{i \in g} G_i\,\mathrm{db}_{g,i}$ and Rademacher multipliers
$G_i = 2Z_i - 1 \in \{-1, +1\}$. Because $\hat\beta^{(A)}(g) \approx \hat\beta(g)
+ D_g$ and $\hat\beta^{(B)}(g) \approx \hat\beta(g) - D_g$, both halves exceed
$c_{\mathrm{cons}}$ exactly when the smaller does,
$$
\{\hat\beta^{(A)}(g) > c_{\mathrm{cons}}\} \cap
\{\hat\beta^{(B)}(g) > c_{\mathrm{cons}}\}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
|D_g| < \hat\beta(g) - c_{\mathrm{cons}} .
$$ {#eq-am-event}
The split perturbation is a sum of $n_g$ independent mean-zero terms with
conditional variance
$\sigma_{D,g}^2 = \sum_{i \in g} \mathrm{db}_{g,i}^2$ — the robust variance of
$\hat\beta(g)$ — so a central limit theorem in $n_g$ gives
$D_g \mid \text{data} \approx \mathcal N(0, \sigma_{D,g}^2)$ and hence the closed
form for the consistency rate,
$$
p_{\mathrm{cons}}(g) \;=\; \Pr\big(|D_g| < \hat\beta(g) - c_{\mathrm{cons}}\big)
\;\approx\;
\max\Big\{0,\; 2\,\Phi\big(\big(\hat\beta(g) - c_{\mathrm{cons}}\big)/\sigma_{D,g}\big) - 1\Big\} .
$$ {#eq-closed}
For $\hat\beta(g) > c_{\mathrm{cons}}$ the two-sided probability is
$2\Phi\big((\hat\beta(g) - c_{\mathrm{cons}})/\sigma_{D,g}\big) - 1$; for
$\hat\beta(g) \le c_{\mathrm{cons}}$ it is zero. No splitting or refitting
enters: a single subgroup fit, supplying $\hat\beta(g)$ and
$\{\mathrm{db}_{g,i}\}$, determines the rate, and a Monte Carlo version that
draws multiplier vectors and averages
$\mathbf 1\{|D_g| < \hat\beta(g) - c_{\mathrm{cons}}\}$ converges to it.

## Calibration: the consistency cutoff as a confidence bound {#sec-am-calib}

Inverting @eq-closed turns the opaque cutoff $p^\star$ into a confidence
statement. The candidate passes the screen at level $p^\star$ iff
$2\Phi\big((\hat\beta(g) - c_{\mathrm{cons}})/\sigma_{D,g}\big) - 1 \ge p^\star$,
i.e. $(\hat\beta(g) - c_{\mathrm{cons}})/\sigma_{D,g} \ge z_{(1+p^\star)/2}$, i.e.
$$
\hat\beta(g) \;-\; z_{(1+p^\star)/2}\,\sigma_{D,g} \;\ge\; c_{\mathrm{cons}} .
$$ {#eq-calib}
The consistency screen at level $p^\star$ is therefore exactly the requirement
that the one-sided $(1+p^\star)/2$ robust lower confidence bound for the subgroup
effect lie above the harm threshold. For the default $p^\star = 0.90$,
$(1+p^\star)/2 = 0.95$ and $z_{0.95} = 1.645$: a $90\%$ consistency rate is a
subgroup effect exceeding $c_{\mathrm{cons}}$ by $1.645$ robust standard errors.
The screen is thus a one-sided $z$-test of $H_0 : \beta(g) \le c_{\mathrm{cons}}$
evaluated with the split-matched robust standard error $\sigma_{D,g}$, and
$p^\star$ is a choice of one-sided confidence level rather than a convention —
the screen tightens with subgroup size only through $\sigma_{D,g}$, so small
subgroups must show a larger $\hat\beta(g) - c_{\mathrm{cons}}$ to pass.

## One apparatus, three multiplier laws {#sec-am-laws}

The closed form depends on the multiplier law only through its first two moments,
$\mathbb E\,G_i = 0$ and $\operatorname{Var} G_i = 1$. Three standard choices
therefore share the limit @eq-closed:

| Multiplier $G_i$ | Distribution | Recovers |
|---|---|---|
| $2Z_i - 1$, $Z_i \sim \mathrm{Ber}(1/2)$ | Rademacher $\pm 1$ | the literal $50/50$ split |
| $G_i \sim \mathcal N(0,1)$ | Gaussian | score / estimating-function resampling [@linweiying1993; @parzenweiying1994; @jinyingwei2001] |
| $G_i \sim \mathrm{Pois}(1) - 1$ | centered Poisson | the weird / wild survival bootstrap [@dobler2017], and the asymptotic multiplicity law of the nonparametric bootstrap |

: Multiplier laws giving the same limiting consistency rate. {#tbl-am-mult}

The fair-coin split, Gaussian score resampling, and the weird bootstrap are thus
three coordinates on one object — a multiplier bootstrap of the subgroup
estimating function. The split is the finite Rademacher member the original
algorithm realizes by literal subsetting; the centered-Poisson member is the one
the post-selection correction of @sec-bridge uses, because a subject's count in a
size-$N$ with-replacement resample is
$\mathrm{Binomial}(N, 1/N) \to \mathrm{Poisson}(1)$, so its centered multiplicity
is exactly $\mathrm{Pois}(1) - 1$.

## The segue to post-selection re-selection {#sec-am-segue}

The screen and the post-selection correction ask different questions of the same
apparatus. The screen is a *per-candidate* yes/no: under a $50/50$ split, does
the effect replicate on both halves? Its answer is the tail functional @eq-closed
of a single candidate's perturbation. The correction of @sec-bridge is a
*competition* among candidates: under one shared perturbation broadcast to the
whole family, which candidate is re-selected, and by how much does selection
inflate its effect? Its answer is a maximum-type functional over the family. The
move from the first to the second is the move from one candidate to many under a
shared multiplier vector — from a per-candidate tail to an order statistic — and
the centered-Poisson member is what makes that re-selection mimic the
nonparametric bootstrap's own resampling. The consistency screen is, in this
sense, the one-candidate, yes/no warm-up for the many-candidate, how-much
machinery the paper builds.
